headline: Europe names five countries to speak for it in the Ukraine peace talks
standfirst: Meeting in Dublin, EU leaders entrusted their voice to Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, and Friedrich Merz asked Donald Trump for “no surprises” before his talks with Vladimir Putin in China. Qatar allies with Turkey as Israel debates a strike on Iran, an outage grounded every flight in America, the Houthis target Saudi Arabia, and in Burkina Faso rival jihadists fight each other.

essentials.title: Europe picks five countries for the Ukraine talks as Berlin warns Washington against surprises
essentials.standfirst: Meeting in Dublin, European leaders entrusted their voice in future negotiations to the EU's institutions and to five members of the “coalition of the willing”. Germany's chancellor has asked Donald Trump for “no surprises” ahead of his expected talks with Vladimir Putin in China.
body: On Friday 13 November, after a meeting of European leaders in Dublin, the president of the European Council, António Costa, announced that Europe would be represented at future negotiations on Ukraine by the EU and five members of the “coalition of the willing”: Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, Al Jazeera reports.

The choice answers America's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the latter having urged Europe to speak with one voice, but Moscow still refuses to involve Europeans directly, with the Kremlin's spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, insisting that no decision has been taken.

Germany's chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who expects Donald Trump to discuss Ukraine with Vladimir Putin in China next week, has asked the American president for “no surprises”, with some in Dublin fearing a “second Anchorage”, according to Reuters, quoted by Al-Monitor.

figure.label: countries chosen to represent Europe alongside the EU's institutions
figure.compare: Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland

positions.wants: To speak “with one voice” in all discussions on Ukraine's future, according to António Costa, through five countries of the coalition of the willing.
Talks focused on the framework for guaranteeing Ukraine's security after peace, with NATO remaining, in Friedrich Merz's view, the bedrock of European security.
A single European interlocutor: that would be greater progress than Russia's acceptance of Europe's presence, according to Jared Kushner.
No decision yet on European participation, according to the Kremlin's spokesman, Dmitry Peskov.

next.t: European Council meeting, with Ukraine's financing for 2027 high on the agenda.

analysis.title: The ghost of Anchorage
analysis.text: The allusion to the summit in Anchorage, Alaska, where Donald Trump hosted Vladimir Putin in August 2025 without the Europeans, betrays a fear of a settlement struck over their heads. Friedrich Merz wants the coming talks to address a single question, the framework under which Ukraine's security would be guaranteed after peace, and rejects Russia's idea of redesigning the continent's security architecture, which in his view NATO already provides, Reuters reports. The chancellor is also pressing partners to write support for Kyiv into the EU's next multi-year budget, a proposal that enjoys broad backing but whose adoption remains distant. He expects genuine peace negotiations to begin in the coming weeks, with Europeans taking part for the first time.

keys.title: Who speaks for Europe
keys.text: Italy's prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, argues for a single European envoy, judging the existing formats too numerous. The EU's foreign-policy chief, Kaja Kallas, claims the role but lacks unanimous support, according to Al Jazeera.

keys.title: Moscow's scepticism
keys.text: The Kremlin has not confirmed that it agreed to widen the three-way talks to include the Europeans. Dmitry Peskov likened European leaders to “spiders in a jar”, according to Al Jazeera.

context.t: Russia launches its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin meet in Anchorage, Alaska, without the Europeans.
Three-way talks open in Abu Dhabi, yielding agreement on a large prisoner exchange.
America's envoys are received at the Kremlin, then by Volodymyr Zelensky near Dublin.
The EU names five countries to represent Europe; Friedrich Merz asks Donald Trump for “no surprises”.

essentials.title: Qatar seals a defence pact with Turkey as Israel debates a strike on Iran
essentials.standfirst: Doha and Ankara pledged on Friday to stand together against any armed attack on either of them, a sign of waning faith in America's guarantees in the Gulf. In Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu's caretaker government is preparing a fresh offensive against Iran, without open backing from the army or Washington.
body: In Istanbul on Friday 13 November, Turkey's president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and the emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, signed a mutual-defence agreement under which the two countries promise a common stance against any external armed attack, Al Jazeera reports.

Gulf monarchies believe America's security guarantees no longer work, according to a Turkish analyst quoted by the channel, as the Revolutionary Guards' navy says an LNG tanker struck a mine in Hormuz and America's military command says it shot down two Iranian drones heading for Bahrain.

In Israel, the security cabinet chaired by the outgoing prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered faster preparations for an attack on Iran, according to Israeli media, though the general staff sees no urgency and Gadi Eisenkot, who is tasked with forming the next government, fears “devastating” consequences.

figure.label: a barrel of Brent crude on 11 November, according to the EIA

positions.wants: To keep working with Doha to prevent a return to war in the Gulf, according to Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
A “strategic partnership” with Turkey, according to the emir, who discussed the priorities for joint action.

analysis.title: Can a caretaker government go to war?
analysis.text: Defeated in October's general election, Benjamin Netanyahu heads a caretaker government until a new majority is formed, which could take months, Al Jazeera notes. Israel's Basic Law leaves an outgoing government its powers, but the Supreme Court imposes a duty of restraint, to which national security is the clearest exception, according to a researcher at the Tachlith institute quoted by Reuters. There is a precedent: in May 2021, already in a caretaker role, Mr Netanyahu launched an 11-day war on Gaza. The bigger obstacle lies in Washington, which says it is betting on economic pressure rather than a large-scale military campaign, and the leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, Avigdor Lieberman, opposes any decision taken without parliamentary oversight.

keys.title: The IAEA's worries
keys.text: In a confidential report, the International Atomic Energy Agency says Iran refuses to discuss monitoring of its programme while it is under military threat, according to AP. The agency is concerned about the enrichment plant at Isfahan, declared in June 2025 but never inspected.

keys.title: Donald Trump bides his time
keys.text: America's president claims “total” control of the Strait of Hormuz despite almost daily attacks on ships. He says he would not hesitate to strike Iran if things went wrong, according to The Times of Israel.

essentials.title: A telecoms failure grounds every flight in America for more than four hours
essentials.standfirst: The Federal Aviation Administration halted all take-offs nationwide on Friday after an outage hit air-traffic control centres. Thousands of flights were cancelled, and a return to normal could take several days.
body: At 3.54pm New York time on Friday 13 November, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted all departures nationwide, citing “extraordinary circumstances”, after a telecoms failure hit the en-route centres that control aircraft at altitude, Al Jazeera reports.

According to the transport secretary, Sean Duffy, switches and routers overloaded with data gave way, without a total loss of communications or radar, and the homeland-security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, ruled out a cyber-attack.

Airspace reopened at 8.15pm after more than four hours, but more than 4,700 flights were cancelled on Friday, according to FlightRadar24, and Mr Duffy, who wants $50bn to modernise air-traffic control, promises a return to normal before Thanksgiving.

analysis.title: Air-traffic control at breaking point
analysis.text: This is only the third time since the attacks of 11 September 2001 that all departures have been suspended nationwide, the previous occasion being an FAA outage in 2023, Al Jazeera notes. The failures appear to have been concentrated in the 21 en-route centres that handle high-altitude flights, according to the expert Todd Curtis, and an aviation-safety specialist is surprised that backup systems did not take over. According to Cirium, some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5m passengers were still due to depart after 4pm, and at least 827 aircraft already in the air were diverted, 670 of them back to their airport of departure.

keys.title: No cyber-attack
keys.text: Markwayne Mullin insisted that “everyone is safe” and that the incident bore no resemblance to another 9/11. The authorities blame overloaded network equipment, not an intrusion.

keys.title: Days to catch up
keys.text: Some 700 flights had already been cancelled for Saturday, according to FlightRadar24. The recovery depends on crew availability, and analysts expect it to take several days to restore schedules.

essentials.title: The Houthis step up strikes on Saudi Arabia as the UN extends sanctions on Yemen
essentials.standfirst: Riyadh says it intercepted drones over its capital and Eastern Province on Thursday, while Yemen's rebels claim attacks on oil and military sites. The Security Council has renewed sanctions on Yemen for another year.
body: On Thursday 12 November the spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, General Turki al-Maliki, announced the interception of drones over the Riyadh region and the Eastern Province, while the Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Saree, claimed strikes on a pipeline, the port of Yanbu and two military sites, Al Jazeera reports.

The attacks target the main route around Hormuz, with Riyadh saying it pumps some 4m barrels of crude a day through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, while Yemen's government forces have pressed an offensive against the rebels since October.

On Thursday the Security Council unanimously extended for a year the asset freezes and travel bans targeting Yemen and condemned the Houthis' escalation, while Riyadh is urging the European Union to add them to its list of terrorist organisations, according to Reuters.

analysis.title: The East-West pipeline, a vital artery
analysis.text: With the Strait of Hormuz all but closed, the pipeline that crosses Saudi Arabia to the Red Sea has become the main outlet for Saudi crude: the 4m barrels a day that Riyadh sends through it amount to about 4% of global supply, according to Al Jazeera. By targeting it, the Houthis directly threaten the world's oil supply. Yahya Saree did, however, call the Saudi accusation that the rebels had targeted the Mecca region on Wednesday a “grave lie”. Yemen's Saudi-backed defence ministry, for its part, insists that its forces are advancing towards their objectives on every front.

keys.title: Beijing's caution
keys.text: China's ambassador to the UN, Fu Cong, said that sanctions are “only a means, not an end”. The Council also renewed the mandate of its panel of experts on Yemen.

keys.title: European reluctance
keys.text: According to Reuters, European officials fear that listing the Houthis as a terrorist group in the EU could jeopardise a future peace process. The EU's spokesman declined to comment.

essentials.title: In Burkina Faso, rival jihadists fight each other while the state fails to regain ground
essentials.standfirst: Since September, Islamic State Sahel and the al-Qaeda-linked JNIM have fought each other with rare ferocity near the Malian border. The junta, which has lost control of vast areas, is meanwhile tightening its crackdown on critics.
body: Since early September, fighting between Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate, and Islamic State Sahel has intensified in northern Burkina Faso along the border with Mali, with Islamic State's weekly claiming more than 400 rival fighters killed on 9 October, Al Jazeera reports.

The rivalry, which dates back to 2019, has already killed more than 2,200 fighters according to ACLED, a conflict monitor, and distracts JNIM from its war on the army, even as the group controls large swathes of the north, centre-north, west and east, according to the International Crisis Group.

The junta of Captain Ibrahim Traoré, in power since September 2022, this month issued “terrorism” arrest warrants for some twenty people, including a journalist from RFI, while 4.5m people need humanitarian aid in 2026, according to the UN.

analysis.title: A war within a war
analysis.text: The clashes force JNIM to divert fighters and resources from its campaign against the armies of Mali and Burkina Faso, observes Heni Nsaibia, a researcher at ACLED, but nothing suggests the state will gain a lasting advantage, Al Jazeera notes. The rivalry is now spilling into Niger, in the Tillabéri and Dosso regions, and as far as Kebbi state in Nigeria. JNIM also extended its presence into Togo and Benin in 2025, and in October 2025 claimed its first official attack in Nigeria. In 2025 ACLED recorded more than 10,000 deaths linked to political violence in Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.

keys.title: Unverifiable tolls
keys.text: Islamic State Sahel also claims to have killed more than 200 JNIM fighters near Kacham in early September. None of these figures could be independently verified, and JNIM has not commented publicly.

keys.title: Silencing critics
keys.text: The warrants target, among others, the RFI journalist Newton Ahmed Barry and a former foreign minister, Djibril Bassolé. Ouagadougou's prosecutor-general added that outlets such as France 24 were in the authorities' sights.
